strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated, practically important problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing in posters, which current general-purpose editors (FLUX.1 Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0) and specialized text editors (FLUX-Text, TextFLUX) do not support. The idea of using user-provided glyph patches as an explicit visual style reference, without font labels or test-time fine-tuning, is a clear and useful contribution.

The dual-stream conditioning design (a content reference poster plus a glyph reference map, both encoded by the frozen VAE and concatenated along the sequence dimension) is simple, avoids auxiliary modules like ControlNet, and is plausibly effective; the zero-shot generalization to handwritten text (Tables 3, Figure 6) without task-specific training is a notable result.

The data curation pipeline is thoughtful: a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR model for ornamental/calligraphic fonts, content-style decoupled pair construction with disjoint replacement text, and two-pronged verification (re-OCR plus DINOv2 style similarity) yield a 100k real-poster training set that mitigates the synthetic-font domain gap.

Empirical coverage is broad: an in-house poster benchmark, the public AnyText benchmark (English and Chinese), and handwriting benchmarks (IAM, CVL), with competitive or best results on most metrics, plus ablations of the font style reference and the text-region weighted loss.
Practical engineering value: DMD2-based 8-step distillation for >10x speedup, and a text-region weighted loss that is simple and shown to improve glyph fidelity (Table 4, lambda sweep).
weaknesses: The headline quantitative claims rest primarily on the authors' own 200-sample in-house benchmark, which is not stated to be released. This weakens reproducibility and makes independent verification of the SoTA claim difficult; the public-benchmark gains, while consistent, are comparatively modest on text-accuracy metrics (e.g., +1.37% English Sen. Acc. over FLUX-Text).

The ablation in Table 4 undercuts the benchmark's reliability: removing the font style reference improves Sen. Acc. (0.9327 vs 0.8334) and NED (0.9734 vs 0.9502). The authors explain that OCR evaluators fail on highly stylized text, which means the very metrics used to claim SoTA are biased against stylized outputs—the paper's strongest use case. A style-aware or human evaluation protocol is needed to support the central claims.

Comparisons with commercial general-purpose editors (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro) are arguably unfair: SkyReels-Text is fine-tuned specifically for this task on curated in-domain poster data with ground-truth regions and reference glyphs, while the competitors are used zero-shot without such supervision. The paper does not clearly discuss this asymmetry or provide region/mask inputs to the baselines.

Several methodological details are under-specified: how the glyph reference map X_g is constructed when multiple regions with distinct fonts are edited simultaneously, how target texts are inpainted into X_ref (by which model), sequence-length/resolution handling when concatenating three VAE latents, and whether the reference glyph must contain the same characters as the target text (critical for zero-shot font transfer of arbitrary strings).

Potential circularity in the data pipeline: the content-replacement editing that creates training pairs appears to rely on existing editing models (implied to be the same Qwen-Image-Edit baseline), raising self-distillation/domain-coupling concerns that are not analyzed.

The handwriting comparison (Table 3) compares an editing model against dedicated handwritten text generation methods, using metrics (HWD, IS, GS) designed for line-image distribution matching rather than editing fidelity; the claim of 'superior style imitation' over DiffBrush should be tempered, and no editing-style metrics or human evaluation are provided for this setting.

No quantitative analysis of the distillation's impact on editing quality (only a speedup claim), and no release of code, models, the fine-tuned VLM OCR model, or the benchmark is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

Presentation has notable polish issues (e.g., grammatical errors, 'optimzer', inconsistent referencing of Seedream 4.0 as [31]/[32], vague claims like 'unprecedented control'), and Figure 3's depiction of the method is quite high-level relative to the information needed for reproduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and under-served problem: fine-grained, font-aware text editing for professional poster workflows, where existing editing models (FLUX.1 Kontext, Qwen-Image-Edit, commercial systems) lack explicit typographic control.

Zero-shot font transfer from user-provided glyph patches without font labels or test-time fine-tuning is a useful capability, and the training-time LoRA adaptation of Qwen-Image-Edit keeps the method lightweight.

The real-data curation pipeline is a thoughtful contribution: using a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR for ornamental/calligraphic text, content-style decoupled data generation with disjoint replacement text, and two-pronged verification (VLM OCR + DINOv2 feature similarity) is more rigorous than purely synthetic rendering pipelines.

Breadth of evaluation is above average: an in-house poster benchmark, the AnyText benchmark (Chinese and English), and zero-shot transfer to IAM/CVL handwriting generation, with results competitive with or better than models specifically trained for those tasks (e.g., lower HWD than DiffBrush on IAM: 1.32 vs 1.41).
On the public AnyText benchmark the gains are substantial (e.g., FID 6.12 vs 13.85 for FLUX-Text on English; Sen. Acc. +7.50% on Chinese), which supports the claim of improved visual realism.
weaknesses: The central ablation (Table 4) contradicts the paper's headline claims. Removing the Font Style Reference yields much better text fidelity (Sen. Acc. 0.9327 vs 0.8334; NED 0.9734 vs 0.9502) on the authors' own benchmark. The explanation—'current OCR systems struggle to accurately parse highly stylized text'—undermines confidence in the entire evaluation: if the primary metrics cannot reliably score stylized output, the reported SoTA on Table 1 is also questionable. The paper does not provide a human evaluation or any alternative style-fidelity metric to resolve this, which is a material evidentiary gap for a paper whose core contribution is font control.

The main comparison is conducted on a self-curated 200-sample in-house benchmark with no stated plan for release, and it is unclear how font reference conditioning was provided to competing methods (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Text, etc.) that do not natively accept glyph patches. Without this, the fairness of Table 1 cannot be assessed, and the 'new SoTA' claim on that benchmark is weakly supported.

Limited technical novelty. The method is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen-Image-Edit with reference images concatenated along the sequence dimension at the VAE latent level, plus a spatially reweighted loss and DMD2 distillation. The dual-stream conditioning is essentially in-context conditioning already available in FLUX.1 Kontext/Qwen-Image-Edit; the paper does not ablate this design against alternatives (ControlNet, embedding modules), so the architectural choice is asserted rather than validated.

Key methodological details are missing or circular: how the reference poster X_ref is inpainted (presumably by the base editing model, meaning a failure of that step cascades into the final result); how multiple glyph references g_i are laid out on the glyph canvas X_g; and how user-supplied crops are aligned to text regions at inference. These are essential for reproducibility.

DINO similarity between generated and reference text regions is a crude proxy for typographic fidelity; it is insensitive to stroke-level font details (weight, serifs, ligatures) that the paper claims to control. A font-classification metric or human study on style fidelity is needed.

Some results are internally inconsistent with the narrative: B-PSNR is slightly worse than FLUX-Text (34.17 vs 34.53), and Geometry Score on CVL is worse than DiffBrush (31.0 vs 29.6), yet the text describes these as superior or 'comparable' without nuance.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a camera-ready submission: duplicated reference entries for Seedream 4.0 ([31]/[32]), multiple typos ('handwrittent', 'optimzer', 'specificly', 'effective meet', 'which may classified'), and the VLM-OCR component is presented as a contribution but is described only at the level of 'we fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL' with no dataset, annotation, or accuracy details.

No failure-case analysis or discussion of limitations (e.g., performance on multi-line text, non-Latin scripts beyond Chinese, or heavily textured backgrounds), which is important for a paper motivated by professional design workflows.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and underexplored problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for poster design, where users can supply arbitrary glyph patches without font labels or test-time fine-tuning. This goes beyond existing glyph-prior methods (FLUX-Text, TextFLUX) that require rendered glyphs in known fonts.

The data curation pipeline is thoughtfully designed: a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR for ornamental/calligraphic fonts, content-style decoupling via semantically disjoint replacement text, and a two-pronged verification strategy (re-OCR + DINOv2 feature similarity). Training on real posters rather than synthetic system-font renderings is a sensible and valuable choice.

Empirical results are broad and mostly convincing: SoTA on the AnyText benchmark (English Sen. Acc. 85.36%, Chinese 77.10%, FID 5.44/5.44, LPIPS 0.0246/0.0192), competitive or superior results on IAM and CVL handwriting benchmarks without any handwriting-specific training, and comparisons against strong commercial systems (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro) plus open-source baselines.

Ablation studies cover both major design choices (Font Style Reference conditioning and the text-region weighted loss weight λ), and the DMD2 distillation for a 10x inference speedup adds practical value.
The paper is generally well organized, with quantitative tables, qualitative comparisons across poster, scene-text, and handwriting domains, and multilingual (English/Chinese) evaluation.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core technical mechanism—concatenating frozen VAE latents of two reference images with the noisy latent, plus LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen-Image-Edit—is a straightforward adaptation of an existing foundation model. The main contribution is data engineering rather than a new modeling idea, which weakens the case for a top-tier methods venue.

The headline comparison (Table 1) is largely on a self-curated, in-house 200-sample 'SkyReels-Text benchmark' that is not stated to be released, and no code, model, or dataset release is mentioned. This raises both reproducibility concerns and the possibility of benchmark favoritism toward the authors' own training distribution.

The ablation in Table 4 is partially self-undermining: removing the Font Style Reference improves Sen. Acc. (0.9327 vs 0.8334) and NED (0.9734 vs 0.9502) by large margins. The explanation (OCR fails on stylized text) is plausible but circular—the headline metrics are then partly measuring the authors' own OCR limitations rather than generation quality, and it is unclear whether FSR actually helps text fidelity or only style metrics.

Comparison fairness is questionable. Competing methods (FLUX-Text, AnyText, DiffBrush, etc.) were not designed to accept arbitrary visual font references, and handwriting models are evaluated under different 'one/few-shot' protocols. The handwriting comparison in Table 3 pits a poster-editing model against specialized handwriting generators, an apples-to-oranges setting that makes the 'beats DiffBrush' claim hard to interpret. OCR-based metrics (Sen. Acc., Spatial IoU) may also be biased when the authors' fine-tuned OCR is used for evaluation.

Some inconsistencies and gaps reduce confidence: the λ=10 setting achieves higher Sen. Acc./NED than the chosen λ=5, and the justification for selecting λ=5 is thin; the 'Baseline' row in Table 2 is not clearly defined; the editing model used to synthesize training pairs (which risks circularity/teacher artifacts) is unspecified; dataset scale details (number of source posters, text instances) are missing; multi-region editing results are deferred to an appendix without quantitative evidence in the main text.

Writing quality needs polish: several typos ('optimzer', 'specificly', 'edtion', 'handwrittent', 'which may classified'), and overstated language ('unprecedented control', 'perfectly aligned pairs') that the evidence does not fully support. Failure cases and limitations are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-served problem: fine-grained, font-controlled text editing for professional poster design, where general-purpose editors (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext) demonstrably fail (Figures 4, 5, 15).

The dual-stream visual conditioning (plain-text reference X_text plus glyph map X_glyph injected via a frozen VAE encoder) is a clean, simple mechanism that avoids font labels and text-specific fine-tuning, enabling zero-shot font transfer from a single reference patch.

Comprehensive evaluation: an in-house benchmark, the public AnyText benchmark (English and Chinese) with standard metrics and third-party OCR, handwritten text generation on IAM/CVL against specialized models, and a user study against four commercial systems. Strong reported numbers across all of these (e.g., AnyText NED 0.9406/0.8764, HWD 1.32/0.89 on IAM/CVL).

The content-style decoupled data pipeline is carefully engineered with a two-pronged verification (content accuracy via OCR, style consistency via DINOv2 similarity), and the accompanying VLM-based OCR model with the SkyReels-OCR dataset is a useful side contribution (Tables 5, 6).

Ablations (Table 4) convincingly isolate the contributions of the font style reference and the text-region weighted loss, including a sensible explanation for why Sen. Acc./NED drop when FSR is added.
Practical inference considerations (DMD2 distillation, ~8s on a single A100, multi-font single-pass editing, paragraph-level extension in the supplement) strengthen real-world usefulness.
weaknesses: Circular evaluation on the primary benchmark: Sen. Acc., NED, and Spatial IoU on the SkyReels-Text benchmark are all computed with the authors' own fine-tuned OCR model, which was trained (on SkyReels-OCR) to parse exactly the font styles their generator produces. This plausibly favors their own outputs on ornamental/non-regular fonts, so the claimed SOTA in Table 1 is not independently verified.

Training data is generated with Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image), a closed-source commercial model, and the resulting model is then claimed to outperform Nano Banana (Tables 1, Figure 7: 60.2% win rate). This effectively distills a stronger proprietary editor's text-rendering capability and then compares against it, which weakens the fairness and interpretation of the comparison and is not discussed as a limitation.

Reproducibility is undermined despite the 'code and models publicly available' claim: the data pipeline depends on Nano Banana (closed source), the in-house 100K dataset and 200-sample benchmark construction are only coarsely described, and no release schedule or link is provided. The user study (Figure 7) omits participant count and protocol.

Technical novelty is moderate: the conditioning is largely VAE-feature concatenation plus LoRA on Qwen-Image-Edit, the weighted loss is a single-line mask reweighting, and DMD2 is applied off-the-shelf. Reference-glyph-conditioned text generation is well explored (GlyphDraw, GlyphControl, DiffUTE, AnyText), so the contribution is primarily data/engineering rather than methodological.

The in-house benchmark is small (200 images), single-sampled, and curated by the authors; the inference-time construction of X_text (who renders/positions the plain-text reference, and how text region geometry is obtained for genuinely new text) is underspecified, leaving ambiguity about what exactly the user must provide versus what the system infers.

Some reported gaps invite scrutiny: FID of 6.12 vs. 13.68 for the next best method on AnyText is a very large jump for an editing model, and the ablation shows the full model's Sen. Acc. (0.8334) below the no-FSR variant (0.9327) on the headline benchmark; both deserve more analysis than currently given.

Comparison fairness details are thin: e.g., FLUX-Kontext-Pro is omitted from the multi-font comparison (Figure 15), and details of prompting/resolution for competing commercial models are not reported.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-served problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for professional poster design, where general-purpose editors (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext) demonstrably fail to transplant reference typography.

The data curation pipeline is described in reasonable detail (Section 3.2 and supplementary): a VLM-based OCR fine-tuned on a curated 40K dataset, content-style decoupled pair generation via Nano Banana + SAM2 masking, and a two-pronged verification (OCR re-recognition plus DINOv2 style-similarity check), yielding ~100K training pairs.

Broad empirical coverage: an in-house poster benchmark, the public AnyText benchmark (English and Chinese), zero-shot handwritten text evaluation on IAM/CVL, an OCR benchmark (Table 6), a user preference study, and component ablations (Table 4) covering the font style reference and the loss weight lambda.

The text-region weighted loss (Eq. 2) is a simple, sensible mechanism for a problem where text occupies a small image fraction, and the ablation shows it matters (Sen. Acc. 0.7928 -> 0.8334 at lambda=5).
Practical inference considerations are addressed via DMD2 distillation with a reported >10x speedup, and the paper claims code and models will be released.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen-Image-Edit with reference images concatenated in latent space (Eq. 1) plus a spatially reweighted reconstruction loss. Reference-glyph conditioning for text generation is well explored (GlyphDraw, GlyphControl, AnyText, FLUX-Text, TextFLUX), and conditioning a DiT on VAE-encoded reference images is standard practice (e.g., in-context/subject-driven editing). The paper's framing as a departure from 'glyph priors' oversells what is essentially another glyph-image conditioning variant.

The primary benchmark is self-curated and the metrics are partially self-referential. The SkyReels-Text benchmark (200 in-house images) is evaluated with the authors' own fine-tuned OCR model (Section 4.3), and the ablations and the lambda=5 hyperparameter are tuned on this same benchmark (Section 4.5), which is also the test set. Claiming 'state-of-the-art' based primarily on a self-defined benchmark evaluated with self-trained judges weakens the headline claims.

Potential circularity in training data and comparisons. Training pairs are generated by Nano Banana and verified by the authors' own OCR model, so the model is trained to imitate Nano Banana's local-editing outputs while the evaluation frames SkyReels-Text as superior to Nano Banana. The 'Baseline' row in Table 2 is not clearly defined (is it Qwen-Image-Edit with the same LoRA budget? An AnyText-style pipeline?), making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed contributions versus the foundation model and data scale.

Dataset provenance and reproducibility concerns. Posters are sourced from design platforms, Pinterest, and Amazon (supplementary Section A). Redistribution rights for such imagery are questionable, and the data pipeline depends on closed, versioned commercial models (Nano Banana, Qwen3-8B), making exact reproduction of the 100K dataset infeasible even if code is released.

Key experimental details are missing or vague: how the three data sources (SkyReels-OCR-40K, AnyWord-3M, content-style decoupled 100K) are mixed and weighted during training; user study protocol (number of participants, instructions, randomization); and the definition/robustness of the 'Spatial' metric (IoU against ground-truth boxes is partly trivially satisfied since the model edits in-place at known locations).

Several quantitative comparisons lack fairness controls. On handwritten text (Table 3), SkyReels-Text is not trained for handwriting yet is compared against specialist models; conversely, on the in-house poster benchmark it is fine-tuned on in-domain data while competitors are zero-shot. The FID of 6.12/5.44 on AnyText versus 13.68 for FLUX-Text is a large gap that deserves scrutiny given the different editing formulations (generation vs. in-place editing).

Some qualitative claims are not fully supported: Figure 4 and 15 cherry-pick favorable cases; failure cases, multi-reference interference, and the acknowledged paragraph-level/artistic-style limitations (supplementary) are deferred to future work rather than quantified.
Writing overclaims: terms like 'unprecedented control', 'paradigm' departure, and 'bridging the gap' are not matched by the modest architectural delta over the underlying foundation model.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely practical and under-served problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for professional poster design, where general-purpose editors (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext) demonstrably fail at typographic fidelity (Figures 4, 5, 15).

The dual-stream visual conditioning (plain-text reference + glyph map via a frozen VAE encoder concatenated with the noisy latent) is a simple, clean mechanism that avoids parameter-heavy ControlNet-style modules and enables zero-shot font transfer from a single glyph patch, including handwritten and calligraphic styles (Figures 6, 13, 14).

Substantial data engineering contribution: a 100K content-style decoupled dataset built with a carefully designed pipeline (VLM-based OCR, LLM text replacement, Nano Banana local editing, SAM2 mask extraction, dual DINO/OCR verification), plus a dedicated SkyReels-OCR-40K dataset and benchmark for non-regular fonts where the fine-tuned OCR clearly outperforms PP-OCRv4/v5, PaddleOCR-VL, and Qwen3-VL (Table 6).

Broad empirical validation across three domains (poster editing, scene text editing on AnyText, handwritten text on IAM/CVL), with favorable quantitative results on public benchmarks (Table 2: FID 6.12/5.44 and LPIPS 0.0246/0.0192 substantially better than FLUX-Text and Calligrapher), a user study with sizable margins (71.8% vs Qwen-Image-Edit, 84.5% vs FLUX-Kontext-Pro), and ablations on both the font style reference and the loss weight λ (Table 4).

Practical additions such as DMD2 distillation (~10x speedup, ~8s on a single A800) and text-region weighted loss (λ=5) show attention to deployment, and the paper claims public release of code and models.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on closed-source, proprietary tools undermines reproducibility and the stated 'code and models are publicly available' claim: the entire 100K training set is generated with Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) and Qwen3-8B. Third parties cannot regenerate the data, and the paper does not (and legally likely cannot) release the dataset itself.

Potential circularity/bias in evaluation: the model is trained on Nano Banana outputs and then compared against Nano Banana; the in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark (only 200 images) is scored with the authors' own fine-tuned OCR model (Section 4.3), which plausibly favors their text-style output distribution on Sen. Acc./NED. The public AnyText benchmark mitigates but does not fully remove this concern.

Methodological novelty is moderate: LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen-Image-Edit with concatenated VAE conditioning and a mask-weighted reconstruction loss is straightforward engineering; the primary contribution is the data pipeline rather than a new modeling insight. The text-region weighted loss is a well-known trick, and the justification for the specific value λ=5 is thin.

The method section does not clearly explain how multiple text regions with heterogeneous fonts are conditioned during training/inference (Eq. 1 shows a single glyph map), even though multi-font editing is a headline claim demonstrated mainly in supplementary Figure 15.

Several evaluation details are under-specified: the user study lacks participant count, sampling protocol, and question wording; DMD2 distillation quality is asserted but not quantified in any table; competitor numbers on the in-house benchmark are produced under conditions the authors control (e.g., prompts for closed-source models).

Some claims overreach: 'unprecedented control' and 'state-of-the-art' rest partly on a small self-curated benchmark; handwritten text generation (Tables 7-8) is qualitative only in the supplement and admits paragraph-level artistic-style editing remains unsolved (supplement Section C).
